old: His heart growled within him like a mother dog protecting her puppies, baring her teeth at a stranger.
new: His heart growled within him: as a mother dog with puppies growls and bares her teeth when she sees a stranger, so his heart growled with anger at the evil deeds being done.
reason: Butler: “so did his heart growl with anger at the evil deeds that were being done” — the simile’s point (what the growling is anger at) is dropped.
Butler: “fifty bands of men surrounding us” — “armed” is not in Butler.

old: give me a sign from someone now waking in the house
new: give me a sign from the lips of someone now waking in the house
reason: Butler: “give me a sign out of the mouth of some one or other of those who are now waking” — he asks for a spoken omen, which ¶7–8 fulfil (“the omens conveyed to him by the woman’s speech”).
Butler: “went out of the court”; ¶30 and ¶35 of this draft and accepted Books 17–18 render Butler’s “court” as “court”, so ¶11 alone diverges.

old: who made me his herdsman when
new: who made me his stockman when
reason: Butler: “who made me his stockman” — accepted B03 keeps “stockman” (“tell the stockman to look me out a heifer”) and accepted B10/B14–B17 use “herdsman/herdsmen” for Butler’s own “herdsman”, so “herdsman” merges two Butler words; Books 21–24 call Philoetius “the stockman” throughout, including the B22 heifer’s-foot callback.
Butler: “Stockman,” answered Ulysses — same reason as ¶16.
Butler: “replied the stockman” — same reason as ¶16.

Butler: “the holy hecatomb” — the GLOSSARY hecatomb row (D3) renders it as a plain “sacrifice” (B03-P007 “goodly hecatomb” → “the fine sacrifice”; accepted B13 “great sacrifices”); “offering” departs from that word.

new: At this Telemachus spoke angrily to Ctesippus
reason: Butler: “On this Telemachus spoke fiercely to Ctesippus” — the GLOSSARY row renders every “On this” as “At this” (applied at ¶6 and ¶20 of this draft, and at 8 of 8 instances in accepted Books 16–18); ¶27 drops it.

old: I’m grown up now and understand good and evil instead of being the child I was before.
new: I’m grown up now; I know good from evil and understand what’s going on, instead of being the child I was before.
reason: Butler: “I am grown up now to the knowledge of good and evil and understand what is going on” — the second clause (he sees what the suitors are doing) is dropped.

old: marry the best man who makes her the most advantageous offer
new: marry the best man, the one who makes her the most advantageous offer
reason: Butler: “marry the best man, and the one who makes her the most advantageous offer” — the draft’s restrictive clause makes “best” a choice among the highest bidders instead of two qualities of the same man.

old: “By Zeus and by my unhappy father’s sufferings
new: “By Zeus, Agelaus, and by my unhappy father’s sufferings
reason: Butler: “By Jove, Agelaus, and by the sorrows of my unhappy father” — the vocative naming who Telemachus is answering is dropped.
'Forced it to endurance' inverts the natural verb construction (forced X to endure); it reads as stilted on a first hearing even though the meaning is recoverable.

old: Anyone else would trust a weaker ally than me, even if that ally were only mortal and less wise than I am.
new: Someone else would trust an ally weaker than me, even an ordinary mortal who was less wise than I am.
reason: Two stacked comparatives ('weaker ally than me' and 'less wise than I am') in one sentence, plus the conditional 'even if that ally were only mortal,' are hard to parse in a single pass aloud. The reworded version keeps the same a-fortiori argument with a slightly flatter parse.

old: Just so, I wish the heavenly gods would hide me from mortal sight, or that Artemis would strike me down.
new: In the same way, I wish the heavenly gods would hide me from mortal sight, or that Artemis would strike me down.
reason: 'Just so' as a stand-alone connector meaning 'in the same way [as those daughters]' is an archaic transitional usage; a contemporary reader is more likely to read it as 'exactly' or miss the callback to the Pandareus story entirely.

old: it puzzled him—it seemed as if she already knew him and was beside him.
new: it puzzled him—it seemed as though she already recognized him and was at his side.
reason: 'Knew him and was beside him' is ambiguous on first read: it could mean she recognized him as her husband, or simply that she was physically near him (which she already was, sleeping in the house). The clarified verb ('recognized') removes the double reading without adding any fact not already implied. [lead: Butler "was by his side"; no added "standing"]
